title: Escalator: take the controls, motor and panels, and leave the step band
summary: An escalator holds a 5–20 kW 3-phase motor, a worm gearbox, contactors, safety switches, handrail belts and stainless panels, but it weighs several tonnes and its steps and chains can run away if the brake or drive is disturbed. A small team can take the controls, handrail belts, panels, lights and oil in a day; the motor and gearbox need a hoist and 4 or more people, and the step band should stay.

steps.text: Decide what you will take before you open anything. Realistic for 3–4 people in a day: control gear, safety switches, lights, wiring, handrail belts, stainless panels and the oil. Needs a chain hoist on a beam or gantry and 4 or more people: the motor (about 120 kg) and the gearbox (about 150 kg). Not realistic: the step band, the step chains and the truss (several tonnes). Leave those.
steps.warn: Never leave a pit open or a step band loose when you walk away. Close up, or fence off, whatever you open.

steps.text: Close off both ends with barriers or heavy furniture and post a lookout. If it is still moving, press the red stop button on the landing and wait until the steps stop. From now on nobody stands on the steps.
steps.warn: A stopped escalator is still a heavy machine. Nobody stands on the steps or the comb plate while the drive or brake is being worked on.

steps.text: Isolate the power. Find the escalator's lockable isolator (in a cabinet at the top landing or in the machine space) and the breaker that feeds it at the building's distribution board. Switch both off and lock or tag them. There is often a second circuit for lights and a service socket: switch that off too. Prove each supply dead with a meter on every phase (see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: The drive supply is usually 3-phase, 380–480 V. If you can't find and prove every feed dead, don't open the pit.

steps.text: Lift the floor plates at the top landing to open the machine space. They are steel or aluminium plates of 20–60 kg: take out the screws or catches, lift at the corners with pry bars or suction lifters, with two people, and stand them on edge against a wall. Put barriers round the opening and light the space with a torch or lamp.
steps.warn: The pit below is a deep drop with machinery in it. Barrier it off, work in pairs, and never lean over the edge while carrying a load. Don't run a petrol or diesel engine in it.

steps.text: Hold the step band fast before you touch the brake, the drive chain or the gearbox. The steps and chains form a long heavy slope and will run down by their own weight if the brake or drive is disturbed. Chain or strap the step band to the truss in at least two places, with gear strong enough for the weight of the whole band, and wedge the lowest steps. If you can't hold it fast, leave the brake, drive chain and gearbox alone.
steps.warn: Never release the brake by hand, and never undo the drive chain or the gearbox while the step band is free to move. A running band can crush or kill.

steps.text: Drain the oil. Put a tray under the gearbox drain plug and under the chain oiler, open the plug slowly and collect the oil in sealed containers. Wipe up drips at once. The gearbox and reservoir hold 10–30 L between them.
steps.warn: Oil on the pit floor and the step edges is a slip hazard. Keep naked flames away from oily rags.

steps.text: Take the control gear. Photograph the cabinet, label every wire, then unscrew the contactors, safety relays, the controller board and the drive (VFD) if fitted. Cut each wire 10 cm from its terminal and keep the harness. Before you touch a drive, measure its DC bus and discharge it if it reads over 30 V (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: A VFD can hold 600 V DC for minutes after the supply is off. Measure first, and don't touch the terminals until the meter reads near zero.

steps.text: Take the safety switches (comb plate, skirt, handrail entry and step sag switches), the stop buttons and the lights from the landings and balustrades. Each is held by 2–4 screws; cut its wire 10 cm from the switch. Keep each switch with its bracket and note where it came from.

Take the handrail belts. Release the tension at the handrail drive (usually a tension bolt or spring: back it off slowly), lift the belt out of its guide at the entry and roll it up. Or cut it through once and pull it out of the guide; steel-cord belts need bolt cutters or a hacksaw. Each belt is a 20–50 m loop of rubber with steel cord or fabric inside, so coil it with two people.
steps.warn: A tensioned belt or spring that slips whips back. Release tension slowly and keep hands and face clear of the nip where the belt meets the drive wheel.

steps.text: Take the stainless skirt and deck panels. Undo the screws along the edges. The panels are 1–3 mm stainless with very sharp edges: carry them in pairs with the edges away from your body. If the sides are glass, leave them: they are heavy toughened panels that shatter into thousands of pieces.
steps.warn: Cut stainless edges slice through thin gloves. Wear thick gloves and eye protection.

steps.text: Motor and gearbox, only with proper lifting gear and only once the step band is held fast (step 5). Fix a beam or gantry rated for at least twice the weight of the heaviest piece, hang a chain hoist, and sling the motor with rated slings. Unbolt the coupling guard, the coupling and the motor feet, and lower the motor onto timber on a pallet or trolley. Do the gearbox the same way. Take the electromagnetic brake from the motor shaft with the motor. Don't attempt either without a hoist.
steps.warn: A 120–150 kg unit that slips from a sling or beam can kill. Use rated slings, check the lifting point, and keep everyone out from under the load.

steps.text: Close up. Put the landing plates back, or fence the opening with solid barriers and a sign saying the escalator is stripped and unsafe. Take down your tags and locks, and leave the step band and chains where they are. Don't shelter or store things under the pit.

notes:
## What's realistic

**A small team with hand tools, in a day**
- Control gear, safety switches, lights and wiring from the pit and landings.
- Handrail belts and stainless panels.
- Gearbox oil and chain-oiler oil.

**Needs lifting gear and 4 or more people, and some planning**
- The motor (about 120 kg) and the gearbox (about 150 kg), each lifted on its own with a chain hoist.
- The brake and the drive chain, but only after the step band is held fast.

**Not realistic: leave it**
- The step band: dozens of steps carried on two heavy chains with hundreds of rollers. You can't move it without power or a hand wheel, and cutting a chain lets the whole band run downhill.
- The truss: several tonnes of steel, often tied into the building.
- The tensioning springs of the step chains at the lower end: stored energy, and a serious injury if one lets go.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Drive motor.** A 3-phase induction motor of about 5–20 kW. It needs a VFD or a 3-phase generator to run. Driven by a turbine and fitted with capacitors, it can also make power (a project of its own).
- **Gearbox.** A worm or helical reducer: slow, high torque. A good winch, mill or mixer drive. Don't depend on a worm gear to hold a load by itself.
- **Brake.** A spring-applied electromagnetic brake with a 100–210 V coil. It holds when unpowered, which makes it a safety brake for a winch or hoist you build.
- **Contactors and relays.** 25–65 A contactors for switching big loads. Check the coil voltage on the label before you use one.
- **Safety switches.** Heavy-duty limit and interlock switches.
- **Handrail belt.** Reinforced rubber strip: conveyor belting, wear pads, gaskets, a patch for roofs and tanks.
- **Stainless panels.** Sheet for tanks, roofing, a solar oven or a work surface. Cut with a grinder or snips; it work-hardens.
- **Oil.** Settle and strain it through cloth; use it as chain and machine oil, not engine oil.
- **Lights.** Small LED lights and drivers.

## Variations

- Moving walkways (travelators) have the same drive and controls with flat pallets. The same rules apply.
- Escalators from before about 1990 can have asbestos in brake linings, gaskets and insulation. Don't cut, drill or grind anything that might contain it; see safety_asbestos_check.
- Older units use a star-delta starter and relays. Newer ones use a VFD and a board.

## What to leave

- Steps, chains and rollers.
- The truss, handrail drive and guides.
- Glass balustrade panels.
